quiz.q: If a program spends 30% of its time in a function and that function is sped up by 4×, what is the overall speedup?
quiz.explain: Amdahl's Law: Speedup = 1 / ((1-F) + F/S) = 1 / (0.7 + 0.3/4) = 1 / 0.775 ≈ 1.29×. The unaffected 70% of the program caps speedup well below the 4× of the optimized part.

quiz.q: Which power component scales with V² × f?
quiz.explain: Dynamic power = ½ × C × V² × f × α. Static power scales with V exponentially via leakage but not with frequency. This is why DVFS lowers V together with f for a cubic effect.

quiz.q: Why is geometric mean preferred over arithmetic mean for SPEC scores?
choices: It's invariant to the reference machine choice
quiz.explain: Geometric mean of normalized speedups doesn't change if you renormalize against a different reference machine. Arithmetic mean would change.

quiz.q: Which cache miss type is most affected by going from a 32 KB to a 256 KB cache, holding everything else constant?
quiz.explain: Larger cache directly reduces capacity misses. Compulsory misses are unaffected. Conflict misses depend on associativity. Coherence misses depend on multicore behavior.

quiz.q: A non-blocking cache enables which capability that's essential for OoO processors?
quiz.explain: Non-blocking means the cache can service hits while a miss is pending, and even handle multiple outstanding misses. Without this, every cache miss stalls the entire pipeline — fatal for OoO.

quiz.q: On a TLB miss but not a page fault, what happens?
choices: OS swaps a page from disk
Hardware or software walks the page tables
quiz.explain: TLB miss = translation not cached but page IS resident; resolved in microseconds via page-table walk. Page fault = page not in memory; resolved in milliseconds via OS handler + disk.

quiz.q: Which dependence is removed by register renaming?
quiz.explain: WAR and WAW are 'name dependences' — they exist only because the architectural register namespace is reused. Renaming gives each writer a fresh physical register. RAW is a true data dependence and cannot be eliminated.

quiz.q: What does the Common Data Bus (CDB) in Tomasulo's algorithm do?
choices: Connects the cache to main memory
Broadcasts a completed result + tag to all reservation stations and registers waiting on it
Carries branch predictions to the fetch unit
Forwards values between adjacent pipeline stages
quiz.explain: The CDB is the broadcast mechanism: when a functional unit completes, it puts (tag, value) on the CDB; everyone waiting for that tag captures the value in the same cycle. The CDB's bandwidth is often a limiting factor in wide OoO machines.

quiz.q: What is the main job of the Reorder Buffer (ROB)?
choices: Reorder memory accesses for better DRAM efficiency
Hold instructions in program order until commit, enabling precise exceptions
quiz.explain: The ROB lets execution be out-of-order while commit (architectural state update) is in-order. On exception, flush ROB past the faulting instruction; architectural state remains precise.

quiz.q: Why does branch prediction accuracy matter more in modern wide superscalar processors?
choices: Modern compilers can't optimize branches anymore
Misprediction penalty grows with pipeline depth × issue width
quiz.explain: A 20-stage pipeline issuing 4 wide loses 80 instructions of work per misprediction. At 95% accuracy that's painful; at 90% it's catastrophic. This is why TAGE/perceptron predictors hit 97%+.

quiz.q: A kernel has operational intensity of 0.25 FLOPs/byte. The machine offers 100 GFLOPS peak compute and 50 GB/s memory bandwidth. What limits the kernel's performance?
quiz.explain: Roofline: bandwidth-limited performance = 50 GB/s × 0.25 FLOP/byte = 12.5 GFLOPS. That's far below the 100 GFLOPS compute roof, so memory bandwidth limits this kernel.

quiz.q: What happens on a warp divergence in NVIDIA's SIMT model?
choices: Hardware serializes both paths, masking inactive lanes
The GPU stalls until all threads converge
quiz.explain: On divergence, the warp executes path A with matching lanes active, then path B with the inverse mask. Half the lanes idle in each phase, halving throughput. Newer architectures have independent thread scheduling that eases this.

quiz.q: Which MESI state allows a silent transition to Modified (M) without coherence broadcast?
quiz.explain: From E, only this cache has the line, so writing it doesn't require invalidating anyone else — the cache silently transitions E→M. From S, the cache must broadcast Invalidate first.

quiz.q: Which is true of x86's TSO memory model?
choices: All operations appear in program order
Stores can be reordered after later loads to different addresses
It requires explicit fences for all multi-thread code
quiz.explain: TSO allows a load to pass an earlier store (to a different address). This is observable in Dekker-style algorithms. ARM is weaker (more reorderings allowed), not stricter.

quiz.q: Two threads each increment their own counter, but performance is much worse than expected. What is the most likely cause?
choices: False sharing — counters on the same cache line
quiz.explain: Classic false sharing: two counters in the same 64-byte line ping-pong via the coherence protocol. Fix with cache-line padding or thread-local storage.

quiz.q: Which statement best captures the WSC design philosophy?
choices: Maximize per-server reliability with redundant components inside each server
Treat failure as routine and tolerate it in software
quiz.explain: WSCs use commodity hardware and assume failures are constant; the software (frameworks, schedulers, replication) handles them. This is a fundamental shift from enterprise 'each server matters' design.

quiz.q: Modern x86 cores translate CISC instructions into what?
choices: Internal RISC-like micro-ops executed by an OoO backend
quiz.explain: x86 decode cracks complex instructions into simpler micro-ops (μops) — effectively a RISC-style backend underneath the CISC frontend. The CISC ISA acts as instruction compression.

quiz.q: Compared to direct-mapped, an 8-way set-associative cache typically has:
choices: Higher hit time, lower miss rate
Lower hit time, higher miss rate
Lower hit time and lower miss rate
quiz.explain: Set-associative needs n parallel tag comparators, increasing hit time slightly, but eliminates most conflict misses, lowering miss rate. The tradeoff is favorable for L1/L2; way prediction can recover some hit time.

quiz.q: In the standard 5-stage MIPS pipeline with full forwarding, which instruction sequence still requires a stall?
choices: ADD R1, R2, R3 followed by SUB R4, R1, R5
LW R1, 0(R2) followed by ADD R3, R1, R4
AND R1, R2, R3 followed by OR R4, R1, R5
quiz.explain: Load-use hazard: LW's result is ready end of MEM, but the dependent ADD needs it at start of EX one cycle earlier. Forwarding can't bend time — a 1-cycle stall (or compiler-scheduled independent instruction) is required.

quiz.q: Why are precise exceptions important?
choices: Required for restartable page faults, debugging, and predictable OS behavior
quiz.explain: Without precise exceptions, you can't restart a page fault cleanly (architectural state past the fault may be inconsistent), can't single-step a debugger, and can't trap-and-emulate. ROB-based commit enables precise exceptions in OoO cores.
